promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Impacts on society and the environment

questions.q: The '6 Rs' framework is used to help designers reduce the environmental impact of products. Which set correctly lists them?
options: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Refuse, Rethink, Repair
Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Return, Restore, Repair
Remove, Reuse, Recycle, Refuse, Rethink, Reduce
Reduce, Recover, Recycle, Refuse, Renew, Repair
questions.explain: The 6 Rs are Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Refuse, Rethink and Repair, used to lower the environmental impact of design decisions.

questions.q: Which of the following is a finite (non-renewable) resource?
options: Crude oil
Wind
Solar energy
Tidal energy
questions.explain: Crude oil is a fossil fuel that will eventually run out, making it a finite resource, unlike wind, solar and tidal energy.

questions.q: A designer chooses to 'Rethink' a product as part of the 6 Rs. What does this most directly involve?
options: Redesigning the product so it meets needs in a more sustainable way
Sending the product to landfill more efficiently
Selling the product at a higher price
Increasing the amount of packaging used
questions.explain: 'Rethink' means reconsidering the design approach so the product fulfils its purpose with less environmental impact.

questions.q: What does a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) evaluate?
options: The environmental impact of a product across its whole life, from raw material to disposal
Only the cost of manufacturing a product
The profit a company makes from a product
How long the marketing campaign for a product lasts
questions.explain: An LCA is a 'cradle to grave' analysis of a product's environmental impact at every stage of its life.

questions.q: Why does using recycled aluminium instead of newly extracted aluminium reduce environmental impact?
options: It uses far less energy than extracting and refining raw ore
It makes the product much heavier
It removes the need for any manufacturing
It automatically makes the product biodegradable
questions.explain: Recycling aluminium requires only a fraction of the energy needed to extract and refine it from bauxite ore, reducing emissions.

questions.q: A company redesigns a kettle so that broken parts can be replaced individually rather than throwing the whole kettle away. Which of the 6 Rs does this best demonstrate?
options: Repair
Refuse
Recycle
Reduce
questions.explain: Designing for replaceable parts extends product life by allowing repair rather than disposal of the whole item.

questions.q: What is meant by a product's 'carbon footprint'?
options: The total greenhouse gas emissions caused by making, using and disposing of it
The physical size of the product
The number of workers needed to make it
The distance a product is displayed from the shop entrance
questions.explain: A carbon footprint measures the total greenhouse gases, expressed as carbon dioxide equivalent, produced over a product's life.

questions.q: How does increased use of automation and robotics in manufacturing most commonly affect society?
options: It can increase production speed and consistency but may reduce manual labour jobs
It always increases the number of unskilled jobs available
It removes the need for any electricity
It guarantees products are cheaper for everyone
questions.explain: Automation improves efficiency and consistency but often replaces workers, changing the type and number of jobs available.

questions.q: What is 'planned obsolescence'?
options: Designing a product with a deliberately limited useful life so it needs replacing
Planning to make a product last as long as possible
Recycling a product at the end of its life
Planning the layout of a factory floor
questions.explain: Planned obsolescence deliberately limits a product's lifespan to encourage repeat purchases, raising ethical and environmental concerns.

questions.q: Why is planned obsolescence considered a negative impact on the environment?
options: It increases waste and resource use as products are replaced more frequently
It reduces the amount of packaging needed
It makes products fully biodegradable
It lowers the demand for raw materials
questions.explain: Frequent replacement of short-lived products increases material consumption and waste sent to landfill.

questions.q: A factory moves production to another country where labour is cheaper. Which is the most likely negative social impact in the original country?
options: Loss of local jobs and skills
An immediate fall in global CO2 emissions
An increase in the price of raw materials worldwide
A guaranteed improvement in product quality
questions.explain: Offshoring production commonly leads to unemployment and loss of manufacturing skills in the original community.

questions.q: How can 'continuous improvement' (Kaizen) benefit both industry and the environment?
options: By making small ongoing changes that reduce waste and improve efficiency
By stopping production entirely to save resources
By increasing the size of every product
By removing all quality control checks
questions.explain: Kaizen uses small, continuous improvements to cut waste and raise efficiency, benefiting both cost and the environment.

questions.q: What is the main aim of the Fairtrade scheme?
options: To ensure producers in developing countries receive a fair and stable price
To make products as cheap as possible for retailers
To speed up global shipping of goods
To increase the use of automation in factories
questions.explain: Fairtrade guarantees producers a fair, stable price and better working conditions, addressing ethical concerns in supply chains.

questions.q: Why might a designer research the cultural background of their target market before designing a product?
options: To avoid using symbols, colours or forms that could cause offence
To make the product more expensive
To reduce the product's lifespan
To increase the amount of packaging
questions.explain: Colours and symbols carry different meanings across cultures, so cultural research helps avoid causing offence and improves acceptance.

questions.q: Crowdfunding is an example of which type of consideration for a new product?
options: A way of raising finance to develop and launch a product
A method of recycling waste materials
A quality control technique
A type of planned obsolescence
questions.explain: Crowdfunding raises money from many people, often online, to fund the development and launch of new products or enterprises.

questions.q: A UK company sources cotton from suppliers who use child labour. Which type of consideration is most directly involved?
options: Ethical considerations about workers' rights
The product's carbon footprint
The product's aesthetic appeal
The choice of manufacturing scale of production
questions.explain: Using suppliers that exploit workers, including child labour, is an ethical issue concerning human rights in the supply chain.

questions.q: How can designing an inclusive product have a positive social impact?
options: It allows more people, including those with disabilities, to use the product
It makes the product usable only by experts
It always reduces the product's cost to zero
It removes the need for any user testing
questions.explain: Inclusive (universal) design widens access so that people of different ages and abilities can use a product.

questions.q: Which of these is a renewable (non-finite) energy source a responsible designer might specify?
options: Solar energy
Coal
Natural gas
Crude oil
questions.explain: Solar energy is renewable and will not run out, unlike the fossil fuels coal, natural gas and crude oil.

questions.q: Why is 'Reduce' generally considered better for the environment than 'Recycle'?
options: Using fewer materials in the first place saves resources and energy before waste is even created
Recycling always sends materials to landfill
Reducing makes products impossible to manufacture
Recycling uses no energy at all
questions.explain: Reducing material use prevents waste and saves the energy that recycling itself would consume, so it is higher up the waste hierarchy.

questions.q: A designer wants to reduce 'food miles' in the packaging they specify. Which decision best supports this ethical aim?
options: Sourcing materials from local suppliers close to the factory
Importing materials from the cheapest overseas supplier
Using more layers of imported packaging
Air-freighting components from another continent
questions.explain: Using local suppliers cuts transport distances, lowering emissions and the environmental cost associated with 'food miles'.
